name: Welsh
variety: Northern Welsh (Gwynedd and Anglesey), the variety of the JIPA illustration (Bell et al. 2023); southern differences are noted
sources: Bell, Elise; Archangeli, Diana B.; Anderson, Skye J.; Hammond, Michael; Webb-Davies, Peredur; Brooks, Heddwen (2023). Northern Welsh. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 53(2): 487-510.
Hannahs, S. J. (2013). The Phonology of Welsh. Oxford University Press.
Ball, Martin J.; Williams, Briony (2001). Welsh Phonetics. Lewiston: Edwin Mellen Press.
Jones, Glyn E. (1984). The distinctive vowels and consonants of Welsh. In Ball, Martin J. & Jones, Glyn E. (eds.), Welsh Phonology: Selected Readings. Cardiff: University of Wales Press.
Mayr, Robert; Davies, Hannah (2011). A cross-dialectal acoustic study of the monophthongs and diphthongs of Welsh. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 41(1): 1-25.
Williams, Briony (1983). Stress in Modern Welsh. PhD dissertation, University of Cambridge.
Williams, Briony (1985). Pitch and duration in Welsh stress perception: the implications for intonation. Journal of Phonetics 13: 381-406.
Williams, Briony (1999). The phonetic manifestation of stress in Welsh. In van der Hulst, Harry (ed.), Word Prosodic Systems in the Languages of Europe. Mouton de Gruyter.
Cooper, Sarah (2015). Intonation in Anglesey Welsh. PhD dissertation, Bangor University.

Grabe, Esther; Low, Ee Ling (2002). Durational variability in speech and the Rhythm Class Hypothesis. In Gussenhoven, Carlos & Warner, Natasha (eds.), Laboratory Phonology 7. Mouton de Gruyter, 515-546.
contrasts: voiceless nasals /m̥ n̥ ŋ̊/ (written mh, nh, ngh), which arise by nasal mutation of /p t k/
fortis against lenis stops, kept apart more by aspiration than by voicing
back fricative /χ/ and dental fricatives /θ ð/
central /ɨ ɨː/ against front /ɪ iː/ in the north; merged as front vowels in the south
vowel length, fully contrastive only in stressed final syllables and monosyllables before /n l r/ (tôn against ton); elsewhere it follows from the next consonant
initial consonant mutations: soft, nasal and aspirate
allophony: fortis stops are strongly aspirated in all positions and may be affricated; lenis stops are unaspirated and often voiceless, with voicing mainly between vowels
the voiceless nasals are phonetically a nasal followed by a breathy or voiceless [h] phase; voicing often runs through the nasal itself (fy nhad as [və nɦaːd])
/r̥/ is a voiceless trill or fricative followed by [h]; /r/ is a trill, a tap between vowels and sometimes an approximant in clusters
/ɬ/ is shorter than the other fricatives, with noise spread over a wide band and most energy around 4 to 6 kHz
/χ/ is uvular for many speakers and velar [x] for others; it does not become palatal after front vowels
/l/ is dark (velarised) in all positions in the north and clear in the south
/s/ is [ʃ] in si before a vowel (siarad)

a consonant after a stressed short vowel and before an unstressed vowel is lengthened: /pʰ/ is 200 ms in hapus against 124 ms in hapusach, /tʰ/ 209 ms in ateb against 134 ms in atebion (Bell et al. 2023)
all vowels are short in unstressed syllables; in the north they are short in every non-final syllable, in the south stressed penultimate syllables may have long vowels
short vowels are more central than long ones, except /a aː/
vowel-initial words begin with a glottal stop
in final clusters of obstruent plus /l n r/ a copy of the preceding vowel may be inserted (pobl, aml, dwfn, llyfr)
phonotactics: /ə/ does not stand in a final syllable, apart from a few unstressed one-syllable words (y, yn, fy, dy)
the letter y is /ə/ in non-final syllables and /ɨ/ (south /ɪ/) in final syllables and most monosyllables
in native words /ŋ/, the voiceless nasals and /r/ begin a word only through mutation; unmutated native words begin with /r̥/, not /r/
gwl-, gwr-, gwn- are single onsets with a rounded velar stop (gwlad is one syllable)

stress.rule: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of words of more than one syllable and stays penultimate when suffixes are added (ysgol, ysgolion); a small group has final stress (Cymraeg, paratoi, ymlâdd), and some loanwords are stressed earlier.
stress.cues: not the usual ones: the stressed penultimate vowel is short and no louder than the final syllable, and the consonant after it is lengthened; the unstressed final syllable is longer and keeps a full vowel. In the classic descriptions pitch is low on the stressed syllable and rises to a peak on the final syllable; more recent data show speakers with the peak inside the stressed syllable.

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none: unstressed vowels, those of final syllables included, keep their quality; schwa (written y) is a vowel of non-final syllables that can itself be stressed
rhythm.notes: In ysgrifen the stressed penultimate vowel lasted 87 ms and the unstressed final vowel 107 ms; in ysgrifennydd 92 and 167 ms (one speaker, Bell et al. 2023, table 3).

length.notes: Long vowels occur only in stressed syllables, in the north only in stressed final syllables and monosyllables. Long and short vowels differ in quality as well as duration, and for /eː ɛ/ some speakers show no duration difference (Bell et al. 2023). Consonant length is not contrastive, but consonants are lengthened after a stressed short vowel (about 200 ms against 125 to 135 ms for fortis stops).

intonation.declarative: rising accents on stressed syllables: low at the start of the stressed penultimate syllable, with the peak late in that syllable or on the following final syllable, then a fall to low at the end of the statement
intonation.yes_no_question: the same accents with a higher nuclear peak; the less the question is marked by words or syntax, the higher the peak (Cooper 2015)
intonation.wh_question: not described separately in the sources consulted
intonation.continuation: not described in the sources consulted; a high or rising phrase end is assumed
intonation.accent_shape: L+H*: low pitch aligned with the onset of the stressed syllable, rising to a peak in its vowel (Cooper 2015, Anglesey); older descriptions put the low on the stressed syllable and the peak on the unstressed final syllable
intonation.notes: The high pitch of the final syllable is thought to continue the final-syllable accent of early Welsh.

phonation: strongly aspirated fortis stops; preaspiration of stops after vowels in some northern varieties
voiceless nasals with a breathy release phase
voiceless trill and voiceless lateral fricative

problems: ch is changed to palatal [ç] after e, i, u (chwech, eich, dechrau); Welsh /χ/ keeps its place after all vowels
rh is [h] followed by a voiced trill; it should be a voiceless trill or fricative, with any [h] phase after it
mh, nh, ngh are a voiced nasal followed by [h]; this is close to the phonetic descriptions, but there is no voiceless nasal phase
dialects are mixed: u and y are central [ɨ] as in the north, but stressed penultimate syllables get long vowels as in the south (tadau, afon, pethau with long vowels)
the consonant after a stressed short vowel is not lengthened
the unstressed final syllable is treated as 'diminished' and given the shortest length value (170 against 250 for the stressed syllable), the opposite of the Welsh pattern
the low stressed syllable with rising pitch after it exists only in the tune for the last stressed word of a clause (intonation 4); earlier words get ordinary high stressed syllables
gwl-, gwr-, gwn- get an extra schwa (gwlad as [ɡwəlaːd]), and final clusters such as pobl, llyfr have no inserted vowel
IPA output is mislabelled: short /ɪ/ is printed [ɨ], short /ɨ/ is printed [ø], and stressed schwa is printed [ʌ]
the clitic fy is given the vowel [ɨ] instead of schwa
good: ll is a voiceless lateral fricative with its own sound sample
penultimate stress, with long vowels shortened when unstressed
th, dd, ff, f and the aspirate mutation spellings ph and th are read correctly
stressed y in non-final syllables is a schwa-like vowel and final y is [ɨ]
a special sentence tune puts low pitch on the last stressed syllable and a rise after it
a list of unstressed function words

notes: Vowel formants are left out: Bell et al. (2023) give plots only, and the tables of Mayr & Davies (2011) could not be checked. Bell et al. write the low vowel as [ɐ] and the back fricative as velar [x] for their speaker; the symbols used here follow the more usual transcription.
